title: WITAWITADD: Episode Two - House Rules
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fg72xV_ZX8g

This episode began life as a review of Order of Vampire Hunters (Dark Gate Games) and turned into something else when Daniel (@dungeondive) noticed he was spending more time on his house rules than on the game as written. So the review became a conversation about house ruling itself.

The Order of Vampire Hunters fixes are worth stealing. The timer is the rule most players bounce off, so in campaign play he made it elastic: clear the den inside the limit and you start the next mission an hour earlier as a bonus. Run over and the game doesn't end — vampires spawn every turn at the entrances the hunters came in through, closing the net behind you. The cost is deferred instead: one random hunter starts the next mission with damaged armour, and three hours over means all of them do. Thematically, they didn't get time to repair their gear. He also lets experience carry between missions, because building your hero is the fun.

The broader argument is that this is simply how RPGs have always been played — no group runs one 100% as written. He acknowledges the counter-position honestly: it shouldn't be the player's job to fix a game, and with so many good games available, why bother? But when a game is two rules away from being what you want, fix the two rules. Talisman, City of Chaos, Folklore and Shadows of Brimstone all get the same treatment, tracked in notebooks.

----

Do you have a game you'd never play without a particular house rule — or are you rules-as-written, on the grounds that fixing a design isn't the buyer's job?
